claims.text: The target materials are noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
Rapid heating and cooling of these nanoparticles typically yields mixed phases.
Rapid heating and cooling of these nanoparticles typically causes elemental segregation.
Single-phase solid-solution selection in rapidly heated and cooled noble metal-based HEA nanoparticles is governed by a transient high-temperature diffusion state.
A brief thermal hold just below the melting point enhances atomic mobility.
Enhanced atomic mobility during the hold enables sufficient mixing to overcome kinetic barriers.
Sufficient high-temperature mixing prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
The controlled intervention is to introduce a brief hold just below the full melting point before rapid quenching.
The intervention produces a transient liquid-like state or high-diffusivity regime.
Extending the high-temperature state produces a more uniform distribution of constituent elements.
Rapid quenching kinetically traps nonuniform elemental distributions.
Reducing kinetic trapping favors formation of a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Held samples will show more single-phase solid-solution character than immediate-quench controls.
Held samples will show less phase separation and elemental segregation than immediate-quench controls.
Held samples will show more controlled particle morphology than immediate-quench controls.
The hold must be short enough to avoid excessive particle coarsening.
The hypothesis applies when processing occurs near the decomposition point.
The hypothesis applies only when hold duration promotes mixing without significant particle coarsening.
The optimal hold temperature and duration remain undetermined.
Failure of the held samples to show a statistically significant improvement in single-phase formation and elemental homogeneity relative to immediate-quench controls would falsify the hypothesis.
